Le rapport des citoyens de Montréal-Nord: The relationship Montréal-Nord residents have with their neighbourhood is very intense, and that intensity is no accident. Alarming social indicators, underfunded community organizations and the stigmatization of the neighbourhood all contribute to the strong opinions North Montréalers hold about the place where they live. Still, just as Montréal-Nord is plural, it holds a wide diversity of perspectives and feelings. In the best cases, there is a sincere attachment to the neighbourhood and a deep desire to thrive there.
Dans le pire des cas, Montréal-Nord devi: In the worst cases, Montréal-Nord becomes a transit neighbourhood where people live only temporarily because of the social and financial precarity they find themselves in. La Converse went into the field to talk with North Montréalers about their relationship with their neighbourhood. We paint a portrait of some of them to show the nature of this complex relationship.
« J’aime la vie », affirme Chance pour s: “I love life,” says Chance by way of introduction. Sitting on a bench in Parc Saint-Laurent, Chance has a radiant smile as he says this. Élie Chance Kwibe is a young man from Montréal-Nord who is studying at Cégep de Rosemont. He hopes to go on later to study business management. The 18-year-old CEGEP student is very active in his community. He works at l’Escale, a North Montréal community organization dedicated to supporting the neighbourhood’s youth. Getting an interview with Chance is not easy, since he is so busy.
Il a finalement fallu s’entretenir avec: In the end, we had to talk to him in the park next to his organization during one of his breaks, right after he had finished organizing activities for young people. If there is one thing Chance loves more than anything, it is without a doubt Montréal-Nord. You understand it as soon as he starts explaining the reasons for his attachment to his neighbourhood. “You just can’t get lost culturally there,” says Chance. The young man has also lived in Anjou and Saint-Léonard, but he did not feel welcome there and did not make friends. In Montréal-Nord, on the contrary, it was extremely easy for him to fit in. The North Montréaler attributes this to the multicultural side of his neighbourhood.
C’est d’ailleurs ce qui le pousse à voul: That is also what makes him want to raise a family there. For him, it is important that his children know their culture of origin, and raising them in his neighbourhood is the easiest way to do that. “For people who were born here, it’s easier to speak their language because they’ll find people who speak it,” he says to illustrate his point. “So culturally, it’s a gain.”

Dire que Monique est enracinée à Montréa: Saying Monique is rooted in Montréal-Nord is an understatement. The senior has lived there for 35 years. The North Montréaler agreed to share her story on the condition that we not use her real name. Monique is therefore a pseudonym. “I arrived here in September 1972 with only $300 in my pocket,” she says in Creole. Monique fled the dictatorship in Haiti to settle in Quebec. Once here, she learned French and started working, for a wage of $1.65 an hour.
« J’ai pu élever six enfants au Canada,: “I was able to raise six children in Canada,” the grandmother says proudly. “Some of them became a doctor, a nurse, a hockey player, an accountant.” After accomplishing all of that, Monique has a heavy heart. “It saddens me to see so many young Haitians in Montréal-Nord who do nothing,” she says. “I have a granddaughter who is about to sign a contract to go play basketball in the United States. She got there because she was always involved in fulfilling activities that kept her away from the street.” That is why Monique is asking political leaders for far more resources and better support for these young people. “There need to be more spaces set aside for sports for them,” she says. “They need sewing classes. They need cooking classes.”
Pour elle, il ne fait aucun doute que Mo: For her, there is no doubt that Montréal-Nord is a place where you can raise children. “I don’t agree with the people who put down Montréal-Nord and Saint-Michel,” says Monique. “It all depends on how you raise your children.”
« Je ne me sens pas encore prêt à quitte: “I don’t feel ready to leave Montréal-Nord yet.” That is the statement Adul makes right off the bat at the start of our interview. Adul Sadiq Adul is a father of four who came to settle in Montréal-Nord in 2002. Immigrating to Quebec was very difficult for him. “Leaving Chad and coming here is a real obstacle course,” Adul explains. “And once you get here, it’s very hard too,” he goes on. “There are a lot of difficulties integrating, especially in the workplace.” The Montréaler tells us he had to go back to school to be able to enter the job market, and today he works as an accountant.
Adul parle de Montréal-Nord comme quelqu: Adul speaks about Montréal-Nord like someone who knows everything about the neighbourhood. “I’ve lived in this neighbourhood for more than 20 years.
Donc, j’’ai vu pas mal de changements et: So I’ve seen quite a few changes, and I’ve also seen quite a few challenges to take on,” he admits. When he begins explaining the reasons for his attachment to the neighbourhood, it becomes clear that Adul loves Montréal-Nord because he found the same social dynamics there as in his country of origin. “I come from a country where people live as a community,” he explains. “When I arrived in Montréal-Nord, I found the same thing. People support each other.” The father agrees with Chance that Montréal-Nord makes it easier for immigrants to integrate. “It’s a multicultural neighbourhood where a newly arrived immigrant doesn’t feel all that out of place,” he says. “For immigrants to integrate well, it’s a must.” The accountant nonetheless acknowledges the many problems Montréal-Nord faces. As a father, he is well placed to see them. “Summer in Montréal-Nord is very lively,” he explains. “But for the past two weeks, I’ve noticed that hardly any cars go by. So people are worried. They’re afraid to go out after sunset.”
Pour faire face à ces enjeux, Adul préco: To face these issues, Adul recommends a behaviour he has always made sure to adopt in his civic life: getting involved. He has volunteered for several community organizations, both in Laval and in his neighbourhood, since arriving in Canada. He volunteers notably at L’escale and Un itinéraire pour tous, two community organizations very active in Montréal-Nord. “You have to fight to get a positive result,” the North Montréaler says to explain his involvement. “You can’t stay in your corner and mope. You have to act, step in, give your time, raise awareness.
C’est avec la petite pierre de chacun qu: It’s with everyone’s small stone that we manage to build something for everyone.” “If everybody leaves, who’s going to work to improve things?” he asks in conclusion.
<strong>Edna (nom fictif), du Chili à Mo: Edna (not her real name), from Chile to Montréal-Nord, by way of Mexico
Edna, une réfugiée haïtienne vivant à Mo: Edna, a Haitian refugee who has lived in Montréal-Nord for two months, admits she is forced to stay in her neighbourhood despite wanting to leave. “I’m not stable yet,” she acknowledges. “I don’t know the country. As a newcomer, I can’t just leave this neighbourhood and go live in another. I stay in Montréal-Nord because that’s where my job is.” Edna’s relationship with Montréal-Nord resembles a love-hate relationship. The two push each other away but end up together anyway, because they are trapped in a dynamic of dependence. Yet Edna crossed four countries and thousands of kilometres to come live in this neighbourhood. The mother first left her native country to live in the Dominican Republic.
Elle a par la suite vécu au Chili, au Me: She then lived in Chile, Mexico and the United States, always searching for a better life for herself and her family. Racism, along with the difficulties of finding work and getting regularized, forced her each time to pack her bags and set off on perilous journeys toward kinder skies. Her husband even had to cross South America on foot, from Chile to Mexico. “It was really hard for him,” Edna explains, a lump in her throat. “Sometimes he had to look at photos of our child to find strength.”
En dépit de toutes les difficultés, Edna: In spite of all the difficulties, Edna managed to enter Canada, where she filed an asylum claim with her family members. She now lives with them in Montréal-Nord. Like Chance, Monique and Adul, Edna is well aware of the diversity in Montréal-Nord. That is in fact what attracted her. “There are a lot of Haitians here,” she tells us. “Thanks to them, it’s easy to find the information I need.”
Trouver un logement a également été plus: Finding housing was also easier for the mother. “To find an apartment, you need someone to sign your lease, or else you’ll have to pay double,” she says. “Another refugee like me signed my lease, which allowed us to get our apartment.” Apartment key in hand and surrounded by her community, Edna began her new life in Montréal-Nord with a heart full of hope… but was quickly disillusioned. The insecurity she perceives in the neighbourhood has convinced her not to stay.
« Je ne suis pas affectée par la violenc: “I’m not affected by the violence in Montréal-Nord, because all I do is work and then go home,” she says. “But I see the police all the time, and I see people fighting.” For someone who has suffered so much to be able to offer her child a better future, Edna bitterly concludes that Montréal-Nord is not the right place.
« Je peux élever mes enfants à Montréal,: “I can raise my children in Montréal,” she sighs, “but not in Montréal-Nord.” Montréal-Nord is plural. That sentence, which we stated at the start, sums up well what we take away from the accounts of Chance, Monique, Adul and Edna. Montréal-Nord does not lend itself to an essentialist analysis. There is a Montréal-Nord where gunshots are often heard, where police sirens never fall silent and where household income is the lowest on the island. And there is a Montréal-Nord where people are surrounded and supported by their communities. We must acknowledge the feelings of those who live in the first Montréal-Nord, and follow the example of those who live in the second.
